title: Disconnected producers and consumers
subtitle: Nothing waits on anything else: the method under most of my high-throughput work

stats.label: tokens per second, five-minute mean on two cards, from about 44,000
batching modes any Function Forge function can run in by configuration

lede: Most pipelines are built as request and response: the thing that wants work done waits for the thing that does it. That coupling is why GPUs sit idle while a producer formats the next request, why a slow database stalls generation, and why a crash in one process takes the others down with it. I build the opposite shape wherever throughput or resilience matters. Producers submit work to a durable queue and exit. Consumers pull from the queue at their own pace. A separate completion path lands results where they belong. No component ever waits on another, and every component restarts on its own. A producer's job ends the moment its work is durably stored.
quote: I cut at the point where the two sides have different natural rates: producers that are bursty and cheap, consumers that are expensive and steady.
evidence: High-throughput batch inference: producers that submit and exit, a durable queue, pull-based GPU consumers and a separate completion path, the shape behind 163K tokens per second from about 44,000.
Message broker and queue design: backpressure by not pulling, local restarts, and one definition of done, an item complete only when its completion is acknowledged.
Asynchronous execution design: decoupled submit-and-exit as one of 3 batching modes any Function Forge function can run in by configuration.
author: Corey James
